questions.stem: A 45-year-old man presents with a history of shortness of breath and the following flow-volume loop is obtained. This is most consistent with

opts.why: Restriction reduces overall loop size but does not usually flatten both inspiratory and expiratory limbs.
Variable intrathoracic obstruction primarily limits expiratory flow, flattening expiration only.
Variable extrathoracic obstruction primarily limits inspiration, flattening the inspiratory limb.

questions.expl: Both limbs plateau in a fixed obstruction; intrathoracic obstruction predominantly flattens expiration, extrathoracic predominantly inspiration, whereas restriction produces a small loop without plateaux.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old female smoker with hypertension presents to the emergency department with a wrist fracture after a fall. She has been increasingly tired and confused over the previous week. Her serum and urine electrolytes are (supplied). The most likely diagnosis is

opts.why: Diabetes insipidus causes water loss and usually hypernatraemia, not the described low sodium and potassium.
SIADH usually produces euvolaemia and relatively high urine sodium, unlike depleted extracellular volume.
Primary adrenal failure tends to cause hyperkalaemia and hyponatraemia, not hypokalaemia.

questions.expl: Low serum sodium plus hypokalaemia is compatible with diuretic use. Urinary sodium below 10 can occur after a diuretic has worn off and volume depletion develops. SIADH generally has inappropriately high urine sodium, adrenal failure commonly increases potassium, and diabetes insipidus causes excess water loss rather than this presentation.
questions.note: The original electrolyte table is unavailable; reconstructed illustrative results are used, so the original answer cannot be authenticated.

questions.stem: A 74-year old man complains of chest pain. An electrocardiograph is performed and displayed here. The occluded coronary artery could be the

opts.why: A diagonal occlusion most often creates anterolateral rather than inferior ST-elevation pattern.
Left-main occlusion causes broader ischaemia and does not characteristically give isolated inferior STEMI.

opts.t: Right coronary or left circumflex artery

opts.why: LAD alone typically produces anterior ST elevations in V1–V4, not the inferior pattern.

questions.expl: An inferior STEMI pattern can arise from either the right coronary or the dominant left circumflex circulation. LAD and diagonal occlusions usually cause anterior or anterolateral rather than isolated inferior changes.
questions.note: Reconstructed inferior-STEMI ECG; original tracing unavailable.

questions.stem: The recommended filter grade of a needle to be effective in excluding microorganisms is

opts.why: A 2-µm filter may pass many bacteria and does not qualify as sterilising grade.
0.02 µm is unnecessarily fine and would markedly limit flow for routine sterilising filtration.
20 µm is a particle filter and cannot reliably remove microorganisms.

questions.expl: A 0.2-micrometre sterilising-grade filter retains most bacteria and is used in sterile filtration. A 2 or 20 micrometre filter would not reliably exclude microorganisms; 0.02 micrometres is unnecessarily fine for this stated criterion.

questions.stem: A patient has severe hypokalaemia and is in cardiac arrest. The Australian Resuscitation Council and the New Zealand Resuscitation Council recommend intravenous potassium should be given as

opts.t: 10 mmol potassium chloride rapid IV bolus
opts.why: Ten mmol rapid IV is twice the cited initial potassium bolus for hypokalaemic arrest.

opts.t: 20 mmol potassium chloride rapid IV bolus
opts.why: Twenty mmol is four times the recalled initial guideline bolus and may be hazardous.

opts.t: 5 mmol potassium chloride over ten minutes
opts.why: Giving 5 mmol over ten minutes does not match the specified resuscitation bolus instruction.

opts.t: 5 mmol potassium chloride as an IV bolus

questions.expl: ANZCOR specifies an initial 5 mmol IV potassium chloride bolus in persistent VF/pVT due to severe hypokalaemia. This is a cardiac-arrest exception to usual slow IV potassium replacement. Other doses/rates do not match the cited guideline.
questions.note: Do not confuse with calcium treatment of hyperkalaemia; the official stem asks about potassium in hypokalaemia.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old man has a loud ejection systolic murmur detected on clinical examination before a joint replacement. A focused transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) detects a calcified aortic valve with a peak aortic jet velocity of 3 m/s. The peak gradient across the aortic valve is

opts.why: 48 mmHg would correspond to velocity about 3.46 m/s, not the quoted 3 m/s.
24 mmHg corresponds to a lower jet velocity (about 2.45 m/s).
64 mmHg corresponds to 4 m/s rather than 3 m/s.

questions.expl: Using the simplified Bernoulli equation, peak gradient is 4 times velocity squared: 4 × 3² = 36 mmHg. The other numbers do not follow from the stated 3 m/s jet velocity.

questions.stem: The current ANZCA guidelines for preoperative fasting of adult patients state that studies have shown that it is safe to administer

opts.t: Clear fluids only until six hours before induction
opts.why: Six-hour clear-fluid fasting is unnecessarily restrictive compared with two-hour period guidance.

opts.t: 400 mL clear fluids up to two hours before induction
Solid food up to two hours before induction
opts.why: Solid food needs longer fasting because it is not a clear liquid.

opts.t: 400 mL milk up to two hours before induction
opts.why: Milk is not classified as a clear fluid in the referenced fasting recommendation.

questions.expl: The period-specific ANZCA preoperative-fasting guidance supported a 400 mL clear-fluid intake two hours before adult anaesthesia. Milk and solids do not count as clear fluids, and the six-hour clear-fluid restriction is unnecessarily long.
questions.note: Follow the local current policy; these are 2022 guideline-era wording and not a new universal maximum.

questions.stem: A two-year-old boy with a history of respiratory tract infection one week previously has just undergone squint surgery. His airway was managed with a size 4.5 mm cuffed endotracheal tube. The surgery was unremarkable. Twenty minutes after extubation he is awake and appears anxious, with stridor and a visible tracheal tug. His oxygen saturation is 96% on room air. The best initial management of this child is to administer

opts.why: Propofol sedation does not directly reverse subglottic oedema and may worsen airway compromise.
Salbutamol relaxes lower-airway smooth muscle and is not definitive for upper-airway stridor.
Nebulised saline may humidify but does not acutely reduce subglottic mucosal swelling.

questions.expl: Acute post-extubation inspiratory stridor suggests laryngeal or subglottic oedema; nebulised adrenaline provides rapid alpha-mediated mucosal vasoconstriction. Salbutamol acts mainly on lower airway bronchospasm; saline is supportive only; sedation may worsen obstruction. Steroid and airway escalation may additionally be required.

questions.stem: You place a paravertebral catheter for postoperative analgesia at the level of T5 in an adult patient prior to a thoracotomy. Two minutes following the injection of 0.75% ropivacaine 10 mL, the patient becomes bradycardic, hypotensive and apnoeic. The most likely cause of the complication is

opts.why: Interpleural spread does not normally cause abrupt total respiratory and circulatory collapse.

opts.t: Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity with convulsions
opts.why: LAST can cause seizures or severe cardiac toxicity, but this immediate high-neuraxial triad favours intrathecal spread.

opts.t: Inadvertent intrathecal spread causing a high or total spinal block
Contralateral paravertebral spread without neuraxial involvement
opts.why: Contralateral regional spread does not ordinarily cause profound bilateral sympathectomy and apnoea.

questions.expl: Abrupt profound bradycardia, hypotension and apnoea minutes after paravertebral local anaesthetic are classic for high/total spinal anaesthesia from dural sleeve puncture or intrathecal spread. Contralateral block and pleural spread rarely produce apnoea; LAST remains an important differential but the triad strongly fits neuraxial spread.

questions.stem: A patient is anaesthetised from the awake state to a state of surgical anaesthesia with propofol or a volatile anaesthetic. As the depth of anaesthesia increases, the patient’s electroencephalogram (EEG) will show oscillations that are of

opts.why: Higher beta activity is not the usual deepening EEG pattern; slow rhythms predominate.
Faster low-amplitude activity is more compatible with arousal/light states, not progression to deep anaesthesia.
EEG evolves with increasing concentration, so unchanged alpha alone cannot describe the trajectory.

questions.expl: Deepening propofol or volatile anaesthesia generally slows dominant EEG oscillations and increases slow/alpha activity before burst suppression at very deep levels. Increasing faster beta activity does not describe the usual progression.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old woman has a laryngeal mask airway inserted for a surgical procedure. The following day she complains of tongue numbness and abnormal taste over the posterior third of the tongue. The most likely site of the nerve injury is the

opts.why: Recurrent laryngeal nerve controls laryngeal muscles, not posterior tongue taste.
Hypoglossal nerve is motor to tongue and does not transmit taste/sensation.
Lingual nerve transmits anterior two-thirds general sensation, not the posterior third.

questions.expl: The glossopharyngeal nerve conveys general sensation and taste from the posterior third of the tongue. The lingual nerve serves the anterior two-thirds general sensation, the recurrent laryngeal controls most laryngeal muscles and the hypoglossal supplies tongue motor function.

questions.stem: The washing process of modern cell savers for intraoperative blood salvage removes all the following EXCEPT

opts.why: Plasma protein content is largely removed by cell-salvage washing.
Washing removes soluble free haemoglobin and debris to varying degrees.
Extracellular potassium is reduced in washed RBC product, unlike intact fetal RBCs.

questions.expl: Modern cell salvage washes erythrocytes and removes much plasma and soluble contaminants; intact fetal red cells are not reliably separated from maternal red cells. Thus washing does not eliminate fetomaternal contamination risk.

questions.stem: A patient with a haemopneumothorax has a chest drain in situ, which is attached to a three-bottle underwater seal drain apparatus. The system is attached to wall suction at -80 cmH20. This will cause

opts.t: Rapid evaporation or bubbling of water in the suction-control bottle
The collection chamber becoming a water seal
opts.why: The collection bottle remains the reservoir and does not become the sealing chamber.

opts.t: Suction necessarily reaching minus 80 cmH2O in the pleural space
opts.why: The water-depth suction regulator prevents wall suction of −80 cmH₂O being transmitted directly to pleura.
Control bottle bubbling does not guarantee elimination of an air leak at the patient end.

questions.expl: In a traditional wet suction-control system, the water-column depth limits suction pressure, despite a more negative wall suction setting. Increasing wall suction primarily intensifies bubbling and evaporation in the control bottle.

questions.stem: You inadvertently place a 7.5Fr central venous catheter into the carotid artery of a patient undergoing an emergency laparotomy for peritonitis. The best course of management is to

opts.t: Flush the catheter with heparin and proceed
opts.why: Flushing a carotid cannula risks embolisation and does not address large-bore arterial injury.

opts.t: Leave it for 24 hours then remove without specialist input
opts.why: Leaving it indefinitely without specialist planning risks thrombus, bleeding and stroke.

opts.t: Leave the catheter in place and urgently obtain vascular surgical or interventional review
Immediate removal and manual compression of the large-bore carotid catheter
opts.why: Pulling a large-bore carotid catheter risks uncontrolled haemorrhage, pseudoaneurysm and stroke.

questions.expl: A large-bore catheter inadvertently placed into the carotid should not be pulled and pressed blindly because of haemorrhage, pseudoaneurysm, dissection and stroke risk. Secure it and obtain expert planning for open or endovascular repair.

questions.stem: A patient in atrial fibrillation with a CHA2DS2-VASc score of 2 has presented for elective hip surgery. Warfarin had been ceased for four days preoperatively and on the day before surgery the international normalized ratio (INR) was 2.1. The best course of action at this point is to

opts.t: Give low-dose vitamin K and recheck the INR before surgery

opts.why: FFP is excessive for a planned elective procedure with time for vitamin K to work.
Proceeding without confirming INR correction risks significant operative bleeding.
Four-factor PCC is rapid emergency reversal, not routinely indicated the day before elective surgery.

questions.expl: On the day before elective surgery, an INR of 2.1 after stopping warfarin can usually be managed with low-dose oral vitamin K and repeat testing. PCC/FFP are reserved for urgent or major reversal; proceeding with elevated INR may be unsafe.

questions.stem: An anaesthetised patient is ventilated and has standard monitoring plus a central venous line. As surgery commences, the line isolation monitor alarms, indicating a potential leakage current of greater than 5 mA from one of the power circuits in use. The most appropriate action is to

opts.t: Turn off all life-support equipment immediately
opts.why: Stopping all essential machines can harm the patient; isolate suspected faulty apparatus selectively.

opts.t: Disconnect the patient's central venous catheter
opts.why: A central venous catheter is not the electrical appliance creating an isolation fault.

opts.t: Disconnect the last electrical device plugged in and investigate the fault
Ignore the isolation alarm because the system is isolated
opts.why: A first-fault alarm requires investigation before a second fault becomes dangerous.

questions.expl: An operating-theatre line isolation monitor alarm indicates a first fault; promptly identify and unplug the offending device while maintaining essential care. The central line is not itself the electrical fault and an alarm must not be ignored.

questions.stem: The dose of hydrocortisone that has equivalent glucocorticoid effect to 8 mg dexamethasone is

opts.why: 80 mg is too small: 8 mg dexamethasone equals approximately 8/0.75 ×20=213 mg hydrocortisone.
20 mg hydrocortisone is equivalent to only about 0.75 mg dexamethasone.
800 mg substantially exceeds the approximate 200-mg glucocorticoid equivalence.

questions.expl: Approximate glucocorticoid equivalence is dexamethasone 0.75 mg to hydrocortisone 20 mg. Thus 8 mg dexamethasone is roughly 213 mg hydrocortisone, customarily rounded to 200 mg.

questions.stem: In the World Maternal Antifibrinolytic (WOMAN) trial, tranexamic acid administration within three hours of birth reduced the

opts.why: WOMAN did not show a protective reduction in thromboembolism as the primary benefit.
Hysterectomy rates did not significantly decline with early TXA.

opts.t: Overall all-cause mortality as the primary significant result
opts.why: The clearest time-dependent significant benefit was death from bleeding, not a blanket all-cause mortality reduction.

questions.expl: The WOMAN trial demonstrated reduced death due to bleeding, particularly with tranexamic acid within three hours of childbirth (RR about 0.69). Hysterectomy was not significantly reduced; thrombotic events were not increased.

questions.stem: Preperitoneal pelvic packing is a surgical treatment of haemorrhage from a/an

opts.why: Pelvic packing does not control a duodenal mucosal bleeding lesion.
Splenic haemorrhage requires splenic surgical/interventional management, not preperitoneal pelvic packing.
Uterine atony causes obstetric bleeding treated with uterotonics, tamponade and obstetric surgery.

questions.expl: Preperitoneal packing tamponades bleeding from pelvic fracture venous plexuses and cancellous bone, usually alongside pelvic stabilisation. Intraperitoneal organ injuries or uterine atony call for different interventions.

questions.stem: The gauge pressure on a gas cylinder does NOT necessarily represent the contents remaining if the cylinder is filled with

opts.why: Helium is stored as compressed gas; pressure broadly tracks remaining gas at constant temperature.
Medical air behaves as a compressed gas, with pressure reflecting contents.
Medical oxygen in standard cylinders is compressed gas, not predominantly a liquid/vapour mixture.

questions.expl: When liquid nitrous oxide remains in a cylinder, its gauge pressure largely reflects saturated vapour pressure rather than residual contents; cylinder weight estimates content. Compressed non-liquefied gases show pressure broadly proportional to amount at a constant temperature.

questions.stem: Maintaining a CO2 pneumoperitoneum at a pressure of 15 mmHg is most likely to lead to

opts.why: Pneumoperitoneum decreases renal perfusion/filtration rather than reliably increasing renal flow.
Mechanically and hormonally mediated vasoconstriction generally increases rather than decreases SVR.

opts.t: A reliable rise in cardiac output
opts.why: Cardiac output depends on venous return and afterload and does not reliably rise.

questions.expl: Pneumoperitoneum at 15 mmHg commonly increases systemic vascular resistance through mechanical and neurohumoral effects while reducing venous return and renal perfusion. Haemodynamic net effects depend on filling status.

questions.stem: Of the following, the drug most likely to cause pulmonary arterial vasodilation with systemic arterial vasoconstriction when used in low doses is

opts.why: Higher-dose noradrenaline can raise pulmonary vascular resistance through alpha-adrenergic effects.
Phenylephrine is a pure alpha agonist and can increase pulmonary as well as systemic resistance.
Dopamine is less selective and may increase heart rate/arrhythmias and PVR.

questions.expl: At low doses vasopressin supports systemic vascular resistance while often preserving or reducing pulmonary vascular resistance relative to alpha-adrenergic vasoconstrictors. Phenylephrine and high-dose catecholamines may increase PVR; dopamine is less selective.

questions.stem: When fresh frozen plasma is administered to treat hypofibrinogenaemia in a bleeding patient, the volume required to achieve an increase in plasma fibrinogen concentration of one gram per litre is

opts.why: Ten mL/kg FFP ordinarily gives less fibrinogen than a full 1-g/L rise.

opts.t: Approximately 30 mL/kg of fresh frozen plasma

opts.why: Five mL/kg is far too small a volume for substantial fibrinogen replacement.
One mL/kg delivers negligible fibrinogen and cannot achieve the target increment.

questions.expl: FFP has comparatively low fibrinogen concentration, so very large volumes (around 30 mL/kg, dependent on baseline and unit concentration) may be required to raise fibrinogen substantially. Fibrinogen concentrate or cryoprecipitate is generally preferable for isolated hypofibrinogenaemia.
questions.note: Estimate only, not a precise universal pharmacokinetic dose.

questions.stem: You review a patient before major bowel surgery. Using the American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology consensus guidelines, you assess him as being at intermediate risk of a perioperative adverse cardiac event. When explaining this to the patient, this best translates to a numerical risk in the range of

opts.t: About 1–5% perioperative major cardiac event risk

opts.why: Below 0.1% is exceptionally low, below the conventional intermediate cardiac-risk category.
Five-to-ten percent lies above the classic intermediate 1–5% category.
Greater than 20% denotes very high risk and is not intermediate.

questions.expl: Classic perioperative risk categories use low below 1%, intermediate around 1–5%, and high above 5%. The Anki recall keyed 5–10%, but that is not the usual ACC/AHA intermediate event-rate category; this is a disputed reconstructed item.
questions.note: The recalled 5–10% answer conflicts with conventional 1–5% ACC/AHA intermediate-risk classification.

questions.stem: Postdural puncture headache in obstetric anaesthesia is associated with a greater likelihood of all of the following EXCEPT

opts.why: Subdural haemorrhage may occur with intracranial hypotension and stretched bridging veins.
CVST is a recognised postdural-puncture complication/association.
Seizures may occur secondary to intracranial complications, unlike infectious encephalitis.

questions.expl: CSF leak and intracranial hypotension are associated with CVST and subdural haematoma; seizures may accompany serious complications. Encephalitis is not a characteristic consequence of PDPH. Postpartum stroke is also a recognised association, so it should not be used as the exception.

questions.stem: A woman with atrial fibrillation has no valvular heart disease. According to AHA guidelines, oral anticoagulants are definitely recommended if her CHA2DS2-VASc score is greater than or equal to

opts.t: Score of 2 as an unequivocal Class I indication
opts.why: A score of two in women is below the historical unequivocal anticoagulation threshold of three.

opts.t: CHA2DS2-VASc score of 3 or greater for a woman

opts.why: CHA₂DS₂-VASc zero denotes very low risk and does not mandate anticoagulation.
Score one is not a definitive Class I anticoagulation indication.

questions.expl: The 2019 AHA/ACC/HRS thresholds recommend oral anticoagulation with CHA2DS2-VASc at least 2 for men or 3 for women. A woman with a score of 2 may merit consideration, but is not the unequivocal threshold in the specified era.

questions.stem: When using cardioversion to revert a patient in atrial fibrillation to sinus rhythm, the direct current shock is synchronised with the ECG to coincide with the

opts.why: The P wave denotes atrial activation and is not the safe ventricular synchronization landmark.
U waves are variable post-T deflections and are not used for synchronisation.
Shock on the T wave can induce VF due to the vulnerable repolarisation period.

questions.expl: Synchronous cardioversion locks discharge to ventricular depolarisation (R wave) to avoid shock delivery on the vulnerable T wave. P and U waves are not synchronisation landmarks.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old parturient presents in labour. She has a history of Addison’s disease from autoimmune adrenalitis and has been taking prednisolone 6 mg daily for ten years. On presentation the patient is given hydrocortisone 100 mg intravenously. The most appropriate steroid replacement regimen the patient should receive during labour is

opts.t: Hydrocortisone 200 mg over 24 hours after the initial 100 mg dose

opts.why: One milligram oral dexamethasone daily is not an adequate short-term stress-dose regimen for primary adrenal insufficiency.
No supplementation during childbirth risks hypotension and adrenal crisis.
25 mg hydrocortisone daily is below stress-dose requirements during labour and delivery.

questions.expl: Primary adrenal insufficiency during labour requires stress-dose IV hydrocortisone, often 100 mg initially followed by 200 mg per 24 hours infusion or divided dosing. Baseline low-dose maintenance alone risks adrenal crisis.

questions.stem: The fourth position of the international pacemaker (NBG) code represents the

opts.why: Response to sensing is the third NBG code position, not fourth.
Chamber sensed is position two in NBG nomenclature.
Chamber paced is position one, not the fourth letter.

questions.expl: The fourth position of the NBG pacemaker code denotes rate modulation (R); the first three specify chamber paced, sensed and response. Confusing these slots gives the wrong code interpretation.

questions.stem: Abnormal Q waves are NOT a feature of the electrocardiogram in

opts.why: Transmural infarction can generate abnormal Q waves from myocardial necrosis.
WPW pre-excitation can create pseudo-infarction Q patterns.
Old transmural infarction commonly leaves pathological Q waves.

questions.expl: Digitalis causes characteristic sagging ST depression, PR changes and arrhythmias rather than pathological infarction-type Q waves. Prior infarction and some ventricular conduction/pre-excitation patterns may produce Q-like complexes.

questions.stem: In a 5-year-old child with severe life-threatening anaphylaxis and no intravenous access, the recommended initial dose of intramuscular adrenaline is

opts.why: 1 mg is an adult cardiac-arrest dose, excessive as IM treatment for a five-year-old.
500 µg is an adult-sized IM dose, greater than the age-band paediatric dose.
15 µg is one-tenth the intended 150-µg intramuscular dose.

questions.expl: The ANZCA/ANZCOR period-specific paediatric age-band schedule gives 150 micrograms IM adrenaline for a child under six years. Adult-dose 500 micrograms or resuscitation-dose 1 mg is excessive in this setting.
questions.note: Weight-based contemporary guidance also applies; use the local paediatric anaphylaxis algorithm.

questions.stem: A four-year-old boy is in refractory ventricular fibrillation. The recommended dose of amiodarone is

opts.why: The drug is administered IV or IO in the arrest algorithm, not IM.

opts.t: Amiodarone 5 mg/kg IV or IO after the third shock

opts.why: 10 mg/kg given before defibrillation is the wrong dose and timing.

opts.t: Amiodarone 1 mg/kg after the first shock
opts.why: 1 mg/kg after the first shock does not match refractory paediatric VF treatment.

questions.expl: In paediatric shock-refractory VF/pVT, give amiodarone 5 mg/kg after the third shock in an ALS algorithm, alongside CPR and defibrillation. The alternatives have incorrect dose, route or timing.

questions.stem: In comparison with fresh frozen plasma, cryoprecipitate contains an increased concentration of factor

opts.why: Factor XI is not enriched in cryoprecipitate compared with its parent plasma.
Factor VII is not a principal concentrated component of cryoprecipitate.
Factor II/prothrombin is not selectively concentrated in cryoprecipitate.

questions.expl: Cryoprecipitate is the cold-insoluble precipitate of FFP enriched in fibrinogen, factor VIII, von Willebrand factor and factor XIII. Factors II, VII and XI remain largely in cryosupernatant and are not similarly concentrated. The recalled choice among factors II, VII, XI and XIII is factor XIII.
questions.note: Cryoprecipitate also concentrates factor VIII, but factor VIII was not among the recovered original answer options.

questions.stem: Jet ventilation for shared airway surgery is traditionally delivered at pressures in atmospheres (atm) of

opts.why: Ten atmospheres is far above the usual supplied pressure for traditional jet systems.
Half an atmosphere is below the usual high-pressure source and is not the recalled value.

opts.t: Approximately 4 atmospheres at the high-pressure gas source

opts.why: 0.1 atmosphere is insufficient to describe the traditional compressed-gas source pressure.

questions.expl: Jet-ventilation systems are supplied from high-pressure gas sources typically around 4 bar/atm, but the operating pressure is regulated and must be adjusted to chest excursion and ventilation. Equating a 4-atm supply with routine delivered airway pressure is unsafe.
questions.note: Historic recalled answer describes high-pressure driving source; patient-delivered pressure is lower and device-specific.

questions.stem: Following the initial subarachnoid haemorrhage from a ruptured aneurysm, the patient is at greatest risk of rebleeding during the following

opts.why: Rebleeding risk is highest earlier than one week after rupture.

opts.t: The first 1–3 days after the initial haemorrhage

opts.why: Days 3–5 are later than the very high immediate rebleeding-risk interval.
Days 5–7 are not the peak risk period for an unsecured aneurysm.

questions.expl: Unsecured aneurysms are at their greatest risk of recurrent haemorrhage early, with risk particularly high in the first 24 hours. Among the recalled answer intervals, days 1–3 capture that initial high-risk period.
questions.note: First 24 hours is the highest-risk subset, but the original recalled choice uses a 1–3-day interval.

questions.stem: The sensory innervation to the larynx above the vocal cords is provided by the

opts.why: Recurrent laryngeal conveys sensation below the cords, not supraglottic sensation.

opts.t: External branch of superior laryngeal nerve
opts.why: The external superior laryngeal branch is motor to cricothyroid, not the supraglottic sensory nerve.

opts.t: Internal branch of superior laryngeal nerve

opts.why: Hypoglossal nerve controls tongue movement and does not innervate supraglottic mucosa.

questions.expl: The internal superior laryngeal nerve provides sensation above the true vocal cords. External superior laryngeal supplies cricothyroid motor function; recurrent laryngeal provides infraglottic sensation and other intrinsic laryngeal motor supply.

questions.stem: The oral morphine equivalent of tapentadol 50 mg (immediate release) is

opts.why: 100 mg oral morphine greatly exceeds the approximate 15–20 mg MME for tapentadol 50 mg.
50 mg morphine implies near-equivalence and overestimates tapentadol's relative potency.
2 mg oral morphine underestimates the expected tapentadol 50-mg analgesic equivalent.

questions.expl: A commonly used conversion approximates tapentadol 50 mg orally to 15–20 mg oral morphine equivalents. Opioid equivalences are estimates and should not be used for direct opioid rotation without dose reduction for incomplete cross-tolerance.
questions.note: Opioid-conversion ratios vary across references and clinical context.

questions.stem: The EXTEM plot from a ROTEM sample is shown. The most appropriate treatment for this bleeding patient is

opts.why: Platelets treat impaired clot firmness from platelet deficiency, not a clot that forms and then lyses rapidly.
Protamine treats residual heparin rather than fibrinolytic clot breakdown.
Cryoprecipitate treats low fibrinogen, often indicated by low FIBTEM clot firmness, not isolated excessive lysis.

questions.expl: The recalled EXTEM tracing shows an initially forming clot with substantial subsequent lysis, consistent with hyperfibrinolysis; tranexamic acid inhibits plasminogen activation and is an appropriate haemostatic intervention when indicated. Low clot firmness with preserved FIBTEM instead suggests platelet deficit, low FIBTEM suggests low fibrinogen, and CT correction in HEPTEM supports heparin effect.
questions.note: The report omits the actual ROTEM plot. This recreated EXTEM hyperfibrinolytic pattern corresponds to the recovered 22.1 recall; original figure not authenticated.

questions.stem: A risk factor for the development of torsade de pointes is

opts.why: Hypokalaemia is a classic torsades risk factor; hyperkalaemia is not the comparable risk in these choices.
Bradycardia and long pauses raise torsades risk, unlike isolated sinus tachycardia.
Hypomagnesaemia promotes torsades; hypermagnesaemia is not the classic precipitant.

questions.expl: Female sex is a recognised risk factor for drug-induced QT prolongation and torsades. Hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia are risk factors, but the recalled options specify hyperkalaemia and hypermagnesaemia. Bradycardia rather than tachycardia typically increases pause-dependent torsades risk.
questions.note: Hypocalcaemia can also prolong QT, but was not among the recovered options; female sex is the defensible recalled single best answer.

questions.stem: In adults the spinal cord usually extends from the brainstem to the level of the inferior margin of the

opts.t: Inferior border of the L1 vertebral body

opts.why: L3 is below the usual adult conus, which normally ends near L1.
The sacral canal contains cauda equina roots, not the adult spinal cord terminus.
L4–5 is a standard lumbar puncture level below the conus, not the normal cord ending.

questions.expl: The adult spinal cord ends around L1 (variable T12–L2). L3–L5 and the sacral canal contain cauda equina rather than the normal spinal cord terminus.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman presents for thrombectomy with left lower leg ischaemia. She has not received any medications since presentation, and takes none at home. The sole abnormality on laboratory testing is an activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) of 52 seconds. The most likely cause of the raised APTT is

opts.why: Von Willebrand disease usually manifests with bleeding, not paradoxical arterial thrombosis with prolonged aPTT.
Haemophilia A is a factor VIII bleeding disorder rather than the thrombophilic lupus-anticoagulant pattern.
Haemophilia B causes factor IX-related bleeding, not an acquired antiphospholipid thrombosis phenotype.

questions.expl: An isolated prolonged aPTT in someone with an arterial thrombosis suggests lupus anticoagulant: a paradoxical in-vitro prolongation associated with thrombosis. Factor VIII or IX deficiency and vWD generally produce bleeding phenotypes.

questions.stem: The manufacturer’s instructions for use of the i-gel supraglottic airway device recommend a minimum patient weight of

opts.why: 500 g is under the intended neonatal device range and likely too small for size 1.

opts.t: 2 kg minimum patient weight for size 1 i-gel

opts.why: 10 kg requires a larger i-gel size than the neonatal size-1 minimum.
30 kg is far above the minimum and belongs to a larger device size.

questions.expl: Manufacturer size 1 i-gel is intended for neonates approximately 2–5 kg. Other weights correspond to different device sizes or fall outside its recommended range.

questions.stem: A derived value from an arterial blood gas sample is

opts.why: PaCO₂ is electrode-measured, not a Henderson–Hasselbalch calculated value.
Arterial pH is directly measured by a pH-sensitive electrode.
PaO₂ is directly measured using an oxygen sensor.

questions.expl: Many ABG analysers directly measure pH, PaCO2 and PaO2, while bicarbonate is calculated using the Henderson–Hasselbalch relationship. Other analytes may be measured by additional electrodes on modern instruments.

questions.stem: The most clinically useful indicator of effective ventilation during neonatal resuscitation is an improvement in

Movement alone does not confirm adequate pulmonary gas exchange.
Skin colour is unreliable and changes more slowly than the initial heart-rate rise.

questions.expl: Rising heart rate is the best early bedside signal of effective lung ventilation in neonatal resuscitation. Colour and SpO2 can lag, and movements alone do not establish adequate ventilation.

30 mmHg suggests marked neonatal hypotension rather than normal awake systolic pressure.

Eye opening is a useful sign of awake emergence.
Conjugate gaze may signal purposeful neurological recovery during emergence.

questions.stem: A man underwent a heart transplant 12 months ago. A drug or therapy which is likely to result in an exaggerated effect in him is

opts.why: Phenylephrine works via peripheral alpha receptors but does not classically cause the pronounced transplant adenosine response.
Atropine depends on vagal blockade, with little early denervated-heart chronotropic effect.
Glycopyrrolate is antimuscarinic and likewise has limited direct effect on denervated transplant rate.

questions.expl: Transplanted hearts are denervated and may show exaggerated sensitivity to adenosine causing prolonged AV block or asystole. Atropine generally has little direct chronotropic effect early after transplant; sympathetic drugs and reflex responses behave differently.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman has had a free flap operation of eight hours duration. She received an intraoperative remifentanil infusion and was given 10 mg morphine 30 minutes before the end of the operation. In recovery her pain score has increased from 6/10 on arrival in recovery to 9/10 in spite of a further 10 mg of intravenous morphine. The most likely diagnosis is

opts.why: Morphine withdrawal usually follows abrupt cessation of established exposure, not escalating pain immediately after remifentanil cessation.
LAST produces CNS/cardiovascular toxicity rather than isolated postoperative hyperalgesia.
Respiratory depression is inadequate ventilation/sedation, not disproportionate pain despite morphine.

questions.expl: Escalating pain despite repeated morphine after prolonged high-dose remifentanil can reflect acute opioid-induced hyperalgesia, although surgical flap ischaemia and undertreated pain must be assessed urgently. Ventilatory depression and LAST do not explain isolated escalating pain.
questions.note: Clinically exclude surgical cause such as flap compromise before attributing severe pain to OIH.

questions.stem: Propofol infusion syndrome is characterised by all of the following EXCEPT

opts.why: Severe metabolic/lactic acidosis is a hallmark of propofol infusion syndrome.
Rhabdomyolysis and CK elevation are characteristic features.
Cardiac conduction changes and failure are recognised severe manifestations.

questions.expl: Propofol infusion syndrome classically causes refractory metabolic/lactic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalaemia, dyslipidaemia and cardiac failure. A primary isolated respiratory acidosis is not defining.

questions.stem: Of the following, the drug with the LEAST effect on serum potassium is

Beta₂ agonist salbutamol moves K intracellularly and lowers serum potassium transiently.
Potassium-binding resins remove potassium via GI tract, albeit slowly.

No neurological deficit is a core NEXUS requirement.
No midline tenderness is one of the NEXUS low-risk criteria.

questions.expl: NEXUS clearance requires no midline tenderness, intoxication, altered alertness, focal neurological deficit or distracting injury. Full active range-of-motion is a separate feature of other decision approaches rather than a basic NEXUS criterion.

Paracetamol is analgesic/antipyretic and has no antiseizure effect.

Diclofenac has a relatively less favourable cardiovascular thrombotic risk profile.

opts.why: Sepsis can kill mothers, but it is not the classic leading cause of death directly from severe preeclampsia.
Hepatic rupture is a rare life-threatening HELLP complication, less frequent than cerebrovascular catastrophe.
Pulmonary oedema is serious but not the most common preeclamptic mortality mechanism in the referenced data.

questions.expl: Hypertensive intracranial haemorrhage is a major cause of maternal death in severe pre-eclampsia/eclampsia. Pulmonary oedema, hepatic rupture and infection are important complications but not the typical leading category.

opts.why: ASA IV implies disease that constantly threatens life, absent in otherwise well BMI 34.
ASA I requires no systemic disease; obesity BMI 30–40 is ASA II in the examples.
BMI ≥40 generally represents ASA III, but BMI 34 without other illness is ASA II.

questions.expl: BMI 30–40 without other systemic disease is listed in ASA physical-status examples as ASA II. Obesity with BMI at least 40 often qualifies for ASA III; the others represent no systemic illness or severe systemic illness.

questions.stem: Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome is associated with each of the following EXCEPT

opts.why: Fragile connective tissue/vessels are characteristic of certain EDS subtypes.

opts.t: Progressive cognitive decline as a defining feature

opts.why: Hypermobile joints and dislocations are core EDS features.
Valvular/connective-tissue manifestations occur in some EDS phenotypes.

questions.expl: Ehlers–Danlos syndromes are connective-tissue disorders characterised by variable joint laxity and tissue/vascular fragility; progressive cognitive decline is not a core characteristic. Reduced local-anaesthetic efficacy has also been reported and is not a reliable exception.
questions.note: The Anki answer listed local-anaesthetic sensitivity; this conflicts with published patient experience and the available choice set, so a more defensible option has been used.

questions.stem: The effect of a drop in patient core temperature from 37 C to 34 C is to

opts.t: Reduced blood loss due to better platelet function
opts.why: Cooling impairs platelets and generally worsens bleeding, not improves it.
Coagulation enzymes slow with hypothermia, not accelerate.

opts.t: Systematic correction of INR measured at 37 degrees
opts.why: Routine laboratory assays warm samples to 37°C and can conceal clinical hypothermic coagulopathy.

opts.t: Increased bleeding despite laboratory PT and aPTT often appearing normal

questions.expl: Hypothermia impairs platelet function and coagulation enzyme activity, increasing clinical bleeding. Routine laboratory coagulation assays are warmed to 37 degrees and may not reveal the temperature-related defect.

questions.stem: According to the Third International Consensus Definitions for Sepsis and Septic Shock (Sepsis-3), sepsis is defined as

opts.t: SIRS criteria alone without organ injury
opts.why: SIRS alone is no longer sufficient; Sepsis-3 requires organ dysfunction from infection.

opts.t: Any positive blood culture without illness
opts.why: A positive culture without organ dysfunction/illness is not sepsis.

opts.t: Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection

opts.why: Simple infection needing antibiotics does not necessarily cause life-threatening organ dysfunction.

questions.expl: Sepsis-3 defines sepsis as life-threatening organ dysfunction resulting from a dysregulated host response to infection, operationally an acute SOFA increase of at least two points. SIRS is not required and uncomplicated infection is not sepsis.

questions.stem: According to the 6th National Audit Project, the likelihood that a patient who reports an allergy to penicillin has a true allergy is approximately

opts.why: The majority of penicillin allergy labels are not true allergy, so 90% is too high.
Below 0.1% understates the proportion confirmed allergic among reporters.
50% overestimates true allergy in most assessed labelled patients.

questions.expl: Most patients who report penicillin allergy are not truly allergic on formal assessment, often around 90% incorrectly labelled. A genuine allergy is therefore approximately 10% among self-reported patients.

questions.stem: The calculation of the initial dose of suxamethonium for a morbidly obese patient should be based upon

opts.why: Adjusted ideal body weight is not the standard suxamethonium weight scalar in severe obesity.
Ideal body weight may underdose because extracellular distribution and pseudocholinesterase are increased.
Lean mass alone may also produce an inadequate initial depolarising blocker dose.

questions.expl: Suxamethonium induction dose in obesity is usually based on total body weight because of expanded extracellular volume and increased pseudocholinesterase activity. Using ideal body weight may underdose.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man undergoes a stress echocardiogram as part of his preoperative preparation before a total hip replacement. If he has clinically significant coronary artery disease, the earliest indicator during his test is most likely to be

opts.why: Anginal symptoms follow earlier contractile ischaemia and are not the earliest echo sign.
Hypotension is nonspecific and may occur later than regional contractile failure.
Troponin elevation indicates myocardial injury after the earlier ischaemic changes.

opts.t: New regional wall-motion abnormality on stress echo

questions.expl: Ischaemic myocardial contraction abnormalities arise early in the ischaemic cascade, before ECG changes or angina, making stress-induced regional wall-motion abnormality the earliest echo indicator.

questions.stem: Regarding the Australian and New Zealand categorisation system for prescribing medicines in pregnancy, Category C medicines are ones which

opts.t: No observed fetal effects in animal studies
opts.why: Category C is not defined by absence of fetal effects in animal studies.
Category C is not an absolute pregnancy contraindication under the Australian classification.

opts.why: Permanent malformations are not required; pharmacological fetal functional effects define C.

opts.t: Adverse fetal functional effects without necessarily producing malformations

questions.expl: Australian pregnancy Category C refers to drugs which, owing to pharmacological effects, have caused or may be suspected of causing harmful fetal/neonatal effects without causing malformations, often reversible. It is not a simple rank of overall pregnancy safety.

questions.stem: An adult male patient has a haemoglobin level of 80 g/L and his blood film shows a reticulocyte count of 10%. These findings are compatible with

opts.why: Marrow failure causes an inappropriately low reticulocyte response despite anaemia.
Pure iron-deficiency production failure usually yields low reticulocytes unless treated.
Red-cell aplasia produces markedly reduced erythropoiesis and reticulocytes.

questions.expl: A markedly raised reticulocyte count indicates an active marrow response to red-cell loss, such as recent bleeding or haemolysis. Underproduction states usually have inadequate reticulocytosis. Haemolysis is an important alternative if available among the original options.

Uncomplicated hypertension is not a neurological demyelinating condition.

Local lidocaine infiltration does not cause the characteristic renal lithium accumulation.

Intracerebral haemorrhage is less common perioperatively than ischaemic stroke.
Subarachnoid haemorrhage is not the dominant perioperative stroke mechanism.

Spinal accessory palsy weakens trapezius and can cause lateral scapular winging.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman is reviewed in the preadmission clinic. She is scheduled to undergo a microwave endometrial ablation for menorrhagia in one week’s time. Her preoperative laboratory investigations include the following blood results (full blood examination and iron studies shown). The most appropriate course of action would be to

opts.t: Routine transfusion of two red-cell units before the procedure regardless of diagnosis
opts.why: Automatic RBC transfusion is not indicated solely for unexplained abnormal blood results.

opts.t: Proceed despite marked unexplained anaemia without assessment
opts.why: Proceeding without characterising important anaemia risks preventable perioperative problems.

opts.t: Use intraoperative cell salvage for minor endometrial ablation
opts.why: Cell salvage is inappropriate for minor low-blood-loss endometrial ablation.

opts.t: Defer elective ablation and investigate significant abnormal blood findings

questions.expl: A significant or unexplained blood-count abnormality warrants investigation and optimisation before an elective minor procedure; transfusion is not automatically necessary, and cell salvage is inappropriate. The recall bank selected defer and refer for haematology investigation.
questions.note: Original FBE and iron-study numbers were not published, so the severity and exact clinical recommendation cannot be authenticated.

questions.stem: The outer diameter of an Aintree Intubation Catheter is

opts.why: 10 mm is substantially larger than the Aintree's approximately 6.5-mm outer diameter.
4 mm is closer to an internal lumen measurement, not its external diameter.
8.5 mm overestimates the outer diameter of the Aintree catheter.

questions.expl: The Aintree intubation catheter has an outer diameter around 6.3–6.5 mm (19 Fr) and inner diameter roughly 4.7 mm. The smaller number sometimes quoted is its lumen rather than external diameter.

questions.stem: Extended life plasma is thawed fresh frozen plasma which can be stored at 2 to 6 C for a maximum period of

opts.why: Ten days exceeds the extended-life refrigerated plasma shelf life in the cited specification.
Six hours is much shorter than the validated five-day refrigerated shelf life.
Twenty-four hours describes a much shorter product-use period than extended-life plasma.

questions.expl: Extended-life thawed plasma is stored refrigerated and has a shelf life of up to five days according to the specified Australian blood-component guidance. It is not equivalent to standard room-temperature handling of thawed FFP.
questions.note: Storage labels and jurisdictional rules may change; follow component labelling.

questions.stem: Created by the Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease, the alphabetical GOLD groups A to D are tools for the assessment of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. These classes are based on

opts.why: FEV₁ percent predicted grades obstruction severity separately; it does not determine the clinical ABCD groups.
Oxygen saturation is not one of the two GOLD ABCD grouping axes.
Peak flow alone is neither symptoms nor exacerbation history used for ABCD categories.

questions.expl: The historical GOLD ABCD clinical groups categorised symptoms and previous exacerbation frequency/risk. Spirometry grades airflow limitation separately, and the ABE framework replaced ABCD subsequently.
questions.note: Historical 2022 GOLD ABCD, not necessarily current grouping.

questions.stem: Red man syndrome as a consequence of vancomycin administration is caused by

opts.t: IgE sensitisation required in every case
opts.why: Vancomycin infusion reaction can occur on first exposure and does not require specific IgE sensitisation.
Delayed T-cell hypersensitivity has a different time course and pathology from rapid histamine flushing.

opts.t: Non-IgE mast-cell activation with histamine release

opts.why: Type II antibody cytotoxicity does not cause the typical rate-dependent vancomycin flushing reaction.

questions.expl: Vancomycin infusion reaction follows direct mast-cell activation and histamine release, frequently with rapid infusion. It is not a classic mandatory IgE-mediated allergy and can often be prevented by slowing administration.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old patient is undergoing a diagnostic laparoscopy. Three minutes after insufflation of CO2 her oxygen saturation falls to 85%. You note decreased air entry on the left side of her chest. Lung ultrasound on the left reveals lung pulse and no lung sliding. The best first action is to

opts.why: Continuing insufflation can worsen ventilation/perfusion or tube malposition and delays assessment.

opts.t: Immediate needle decompression despite lung pulse
opts.why: A lung pulse supports pleural apposition and makes pneumothorax at that point less likely.
Contralateral chest tube is unjustified without evidence of pneumothorax or tension.

opts.t: Ask the surgeon to release pneumoperitoneum and reassess tube position

questions.expl: New unilateral reduced air entry after insufflation with a lung pulse and absent sliding suggests non-ventilated lung from mainstem intubation or pressure effects rather than pneumothorax. Release pneumoperitoneum, oxygenate and reassess ETT depth; lung pulse strongly argues against pneumothorax at that site.
questions.note: Recalled answer varied between deflation and tube withdrawal; both are considered in immediate troubleshooting.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old patient presents with exertional syncope. The most likely diagnosis is

opts.why: Vasovagal episodes are possible but do not account for a recalled structural cardiac concern with exertional syncope.
Isolated hypertension does not explain activity-related sudden syncope in a young adult.
Sinus bradycardia alone is not the characteristic exertional outflow-obstruction phenotype.

questions.expl: Exertional syncope in a young adult raises concern for dynamic LV outflow obstruction from HOCM. Other dangerous diagnoses exist, so the question requires the original ECG or clinical data to identify HOCM uniquely.
questions.note: Original diagnostic figure or additional findings not published; practice interpretation inferred from recall.

questions.stem: Bowel preparation prior to elective colorectal surgery is associated with

opts.t: Reliably reduces mortality in every colorectal operation
opts.why: Mechanical bowel prep alone does not reliably reduce all-cause mortality in every colorectal procedure.
Prep without prophylactic antibiotics does not abolish surgical-site infections.

opts.t: Avoids the need for any oral antibiotic prophylaxis
opts.why: Oral antibiotics may provide independent benefit alongside mechanical preparation and are not made unnecessary.

questions.expl: Mechanical bowel preparation can facilitate intraoperative colonoscopy and certain operative techniques. Evidence for reduction of SSI or leak depends on combination with oral antibiotics and operation type; it does not reliably lower mortality by itself.

questions.stem: The part of the lung that is typically divided into apical, anterior and posterior segments is the

opts.why: The right middle lobe has medial and lateral segments, not three upper-lobe segments.
Left lower lobe has superior/basal subdivisions, not isolated apical/anterior/posterior upper-lobe segments.
Right lower lobe has superior and four basal segments.

questions.expl: The right upper lobe has apical, anterior and posterior bronchopulmonary segments. The middle lobe has medial/lateral segments, and lower lobes have superior and basal divisions.

questions.stem: The most common cause of bilateral blindness following spinal surgery and anaesthesia is

opts.why: Retinal detachment is an uncommon cause of perioperative post-spine blindness.
Bilateral acute angle closure is rare and presents with pain and ocular findings.

opts.t: Bilateral central retinal artery occlusion as the usual mechanism
opts.why: Central retinal artery occlusion is less common and often unilateral with external globe pressure.

questions.expl: Perioperative visual loss after prone spinal surgery most often involves ischaemic optic neuropathy, particularly posterior ION. Retinal artery occlusion is rarer, often unilateral and associated with external eye compression.

questions.stem: The 2012 Berlin definition of the Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) defines moderate disease as one with a PaO2 / FiO2 ratio (in mmHg) of

opts.why: A ratio above 300 does not satisfy the Berlin oxygenation definition of ARDS.

opts.t: Any PaO2/FiO2 in the absence of PEEP
opts.why: Berlin requires at least 5 cmH₂O PEEP/CPAP for mild-to-moderate-severe categories.
A ratio ≤100 defines severe, not moderate, ARDS.

opts.t: PaO2/FiO2 greater than 100 and at most 200 mmHg

questions.expl: The Berlin ARDS criteria define moderate impairment as 100 < PaO2/FiO2 ≤ 200 mmHg with PEEP/CPAP at least 5 cmH2O. Ratios below 100 are severe, 200–300 mild, and PEEP criteria must be met.

questions.stem: This image is an apical four chamber view obtained by transthoracic echocardiography. The artery that supplies the area indicated by the arrow is the

opts.why: RCA more often supplies RV and inferior LV depending on dominance, not the typical LV apex.
LCx generally perfuses lateral/posterolateral territory rather than anterior septal apex.
PDA supplies the inferior/posterior septal region, not the characteristic LAD-supplied apex.

questions.expl: The LAD typically supplies the LV apex and anterior interventricular septum. The right or circumflex arteries more often supply inferior/posterolateral regions depending on coronary dominance.

questions.stem: A patient has undergone a multilevel cervical spine fusion and upon emergence from anaesthesia reports complete visual loss. Fundoscopic examination shows a pale optic disc with haemorrhages. This supports a diagnosis of

opts.why: CRAO shows retinal pallor/cherry-red spot rather than the typical optic-disc swelling of AION.
Occipital cortical injury usually preserves fundal appearance and pupillary reflexes.
Posterior ION initially has a normal optic disc, unlike the abnormal disc described.

questions.expl: Anterior ION causes acute visual loss with an abnormal swollen optic disc that may show peripapillary haemorrhages and later pallor. Posterior ION initially has normal fundus; CRAO classically produces retinal pallor and a cherry-red spot.
questions.note: The Anki recall keyed CRAO, which conflicts with the described optic-disc haemorrhages; corrected using ophthalmic signs.

questions.stem: An asymptomatic 65-year-old male with squamous cell carcinoma of the left lung has been referred for assessment of suitability for lung resection. There is no evidence of spread on computerised tomography scanning. PaCO2, electrocardiogram, full blood count and electrolytes are normal. His SpO2 on room air is 95%. His forced expiratory volume in one second is 2.3 litres (predicted 3.3 litres) and forced vital capacity is 3.4 litres (predicted 4.4 litres). The most appropriate course of action is to

opts.t: Exclude all lung resection solely because FEV1 is below 80% predicted
opts.why: FEV₁ below 80% alone requires more evaluation, not automatic exclusion from lobectomy.

opts.t: Require chemotherapy without further operability assessment
opts.why: Chemotherapy decisions depend on oncological stage and cannot substitute for physiological operability assessment.

opts.t: Accept pneumonectomy without assessing predicted postoperative function
opts.why: Predicted postoperative function is essential before assuming pneumonectomy is safe.

opts.t: Proceed to calculate predicted postoperative function and consider resection if adequate

questions.expl: For potential lung resection, use FEV1 and DLCO with predicted postoperative measurements and exercise capacity to determine suitability. This patient's FEV1 is ~70% predicted; that alone neither forbids lobectomy nor establishes pneumonectomy fitness.
questions.note: Recall suggests acceptance, but precise procedure and DLCO are unspecified; safest reconstruction is assessment of predicted postoperative function.

questions.stem: Findings associated with massive pericardial tamponade include

opts.why: Tamponade requires pericardial fluid or other compressive contents, not a reliably dry pericardium.

opts.t: Increased LV filling from external compression
opts.why: External pressure impairs rather than increases ventricular filling.

opts.t: Hypotension, raised JVP and pulsus paradoxus

opts.why: Systemic hypotension and raised JVP are more characteristic than hypertension with low venous pressure.

questions.expl: Cardiac tamponade impairs diastolic filling, causing reduced output, hypotension, elevated systemic venous pressures and often pulsus paradoxus. Electrical alternans may be present with large effusion. Bradycardia is less typical than tachycardia.
questions.note: Original choices not supplied; reconstructed positive-finding question.

questions.stem: The first-line drug recommended by both the Australian Resuscitation Council and the New Zealand Resuscitation Council to treat severe cyanide poisoning is

opts.why: Methylene blue treats methaemoglobinaemia, not cyanide poisoning.
Atropine treats muscarinic cholinergic effects and has no cyanide-binding activity.
Calcium chloride stabilises selected electrolyte/cardiac states, not cyanide detoxification.

questions.expl: Hydroxocobalamin is first-line specific antidote for severe cyanide poisoning, binding cyanide to form cyanocobalamin. Sodium thiosulfate may be used as an adjunct; the listed alternatives do not have equivalent antidotal action.

questions.stem: Complications of severe anorexia nervosa (body weight < 40% ideal) include all of the following EXCEPT

opts.why: Delayed gastric emptying is common from severe malnutrition-related GI dysmotility.
Hypokalaemia may occur from malnutrition, vomiting or laxative use.
Cardiomyopathy/cardiac atrophy can complicate extreme anorexia.

questions.expl: Severe anorexia causes hypokalaemia, gastrointestinal dysmotility, cardiac atrophy/arrhythmias and endocrine disturbances. Hypercalcaemia is not the classic expected electrolyte abnormality (though exceptions can occur).

questions.stem: A patient requires a peripherally inserted central venous catheter. Electrocardiographic (ECG)- aided tip localisation is used to site the tip of the catheter. The initial ECG from the catheter is shown. The ECG when the catheter is placed appropriately will be

opts.t: Absence of visible P waves in all leads
opts.why: P waves become more prominent near the CAJ rather than disappearing entirely.

opts.t: Progressively inverted P waves in the right ventricle
opts.why: P-wave inversion suggests atrial over-advancement rather than optimal tip location.

opts.t: The maximal upright intracavitary P wave at the cavoatrial junction
A broad QRS as the primary landmark
opts.why: QRS widening does not define the cavoatrial junction in intracavitary ECG guidance.

questions.expl: As a PICC tip approaches the cavoatrial junction, intracavitary P-wave amplitude increases and is usually maximal at the optimal tip level; progression into the atrium can make it biphasic or inverted. QRS width is not the placement signal.
questions.note: Actual serial tracings are unrecoverable; a representative schematic is used.

questions.stem: You are asked to review a patient two days after a surgically difficult total knee replacement that was undertaken under tourniquet. The anaesthesia and analgesia technique used was spinal anaesthesia in combination with an ultrasound-guided adductor canal block and high-volume local anaesthetic infiltration by the surgeon. The patient complains of a new onset of leg weakness on the operative side. The nerve LEAST likely to be involved in this weakness is the

opts.why: Sciatic injury may cause hamstring and distal limb motor weakness.
Common peroneal injury causes foot dorsiflexion weakness/foot drop.
Femoral nerve injury can impair quadriceps and knee extension.

questions.expl: The saphenous nerve is a purely sensory femoral branch, so isolated injury would not cause true leg muscle weakness. Femoral, sciatic and peroneal motor injuries could.

questions.stem: When using an endotracheal tube in an adult, the highest recommended cuff pressure to avoid mucosal ischaemia is

opts.why: 50 cmH₂O risks exceeding mucosal capillary perfusion pressure.
10 cmH₂O often underinflates the cuff and risks leak/aspiration.
70 cmH₂O is markedly above mucosal ischaemia-risk thresholds.

questions.expl: Adult tracheal-tube cuff pressures are usually kept around 20–30 cmH2O. Higher pressures can compromise tracheal mucosal blood flow; a target below 10 may fail to provide an effective seal.

opts.why: Flecainide sodium-channel block can raise defibrillation threshold.
Lidocaine may increase defibrillation requirements depending on timing and dose.
Chronic amiodarone can raise ICD shock thresholds and warrants testing when relevant.

Radial arises from posterior cord and courses posterior arm.

questions.stem: A test for a condition which has a prevalence of 1 in 1000 has a sensitivity of 100% and a specificity of 90%. The probability of a patient who receives a positive result actually having the condition is

opts.why: 90% ignores low prevalence and approximately 100 false positives per true positive.
50% is far above the PPV when only 1/1000 has disease.
10% remains too high once false positives in 999 non-cases are counted.

questions.expl: For 1000 people with 1 true case, sensitivity 100% detects one true positive. Specificity 90% yields about 100 false positives among the 999 without disease. PPV ≈ 1/(1+100) ≈ 1%, demonstrating base-rate effect.

opts.why: Right atrial enlargement changes right cardiac contour rather than left appendage/double-border appearance.
Ascending aortic dilatation produces upper mediastinal widening rather than left atrial double density.
Right ventricular enlargement changes the cardiac silhouette/retrosternal space, not the described LA signs.

questions.expl: A prominent left atrial appendage and double right-heart border suggest left atrial enlargement in the reconstructed radiograph. These are not features that alone identify the other chamber enlargements.

questions.stem: Your patient has been administered 50 mL of oral 5-aminolevulinic acid hydrochloride (Gliolan) three hours prior to her scheduled craniotomy for resection of a glioblastoma. Care should be taken perioperatively to avoid the adverse effect of

opts.why: Bradycardia is not the defining expected risk from ALA photosensitiser.
ALA is not a malignant-hyperthermia triggering agent.
Routine RBC transfusion does not cause universal acute haemolysis after ALA.

opts.t: Photosensitivity requiring avoidance of strong light for 24 hours

questions.expl: Oral 5-aminolevulinic acid is metabolised to fluorescent porphyrins; temporary systemic photosensitivity can follow. Avoid bright light exposure for at least the specified interval. Hypotension may also occur but is not the distinguishing photodynamic risk.

questions.stem: Anaesthesia-induced rhabdomyolysis differs from malignant hyperthermia in that it is NOT

opts.t: Reduced myoglobin release compared with malignant hyperthermia

opts.why: AIR typically lacks pronounced uncontrolled hypermetabolic CO₂ generation compared with MH.
Less severe early hypercapnia is a difference often used to separate AIR from MH.
Generalised sustained muscle rigidity is less typical of AIR than classic MH.

questions.expl: Anaesthesia-induced rhabdomyolysis can release large amounts of myoglobin just as MH can, so reduced myoglobin release is not a reliable differentiator. Unlike MH, AIR generally lacks the characteristic severe hypermetabolic CO2 production and generalised muscle rigidity.
questions.note: This is the unusual NOT question; reconstructed choices follow independently recalled wording.

questions.stem: You are planning to perform a peribulbar block and wish to check the axial length of the eye prior to proceeding. The average axial length of the globe in adults as measured by ultrasound is

opts.why: 38 mm represents extreme globe elongation, far above average adult axial length.
12 mm grossly underestimates normal adult globe length.
32 mm is exceptionally myopic/elongated, not the population average.

questions.expl: Mean adult ocular axial length is around 23–24 mm. A markedly elongated myopic globe increases globe-perforation risk during orbital blocks; the other lengths are outside typical adult values.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man suffers a 30% total body surface area burn. A physiological change expected within the first 24 hours is

opts.why: The hyperdynamic phase develops later, usually after initial resuscitation.

opts.t: Immediate increased cardiac output despite hypovolaemia
opts.why: Early low volume/cardiac output prevents sustained immediate increase in output.

opts.t: Reduced hepatic perfusion in the initial burn-shock phase
Immediate marked reduction in systemic vascular resistance
opts.why: Burn shock tends to increase SVR early, not immediately decrease it markedly.

questions.expl: The first 24 hours of a major burn is a low-output phase with reduced intravascular volume, impaired organ perfusion, increased systemic resistance and capillary leak. Hyperdynamic high-output physiology tends to develop after resuscitation over 24–48 hours.

questions.stem: Of the following clinical conditions, difficult intubation is LEAST likely to be associated with

opts.why: Hurler mucopolysaccharidosis commonly produces macroglossia, stiffness and difficult airway.
Pierre Robin micrognathia/glossoptosis commonly complicates intubation.

opts.t: Apert syndrome relative to the other syndromes listed

opts.why: Treacher Collins mandibulofacial hypoplasia is strongly linked to difficult laryngoscopy.

questions.expl: Pierre Robin, Treacher Collins and mucopolysaccharidosis often present marked difficult laryngoscopy/airway obstruction. Apert syndrome can also cause airway difficulty from midface hypoplasia, but is the recalled least-likely among these choices.
questions.note: Relative-risk question: all listed syndromes can complicate airway management.

questions.stem: Somatosensory evoked potentials (SSEPs) are used to monitor spinal cord function during scoliosis surgery. They are LEAST affected by

opts.why: Volatiles depress cortical SSEP amplitude/latency in a dose-dependent way.
Propofol also affects SSEPs, although often more predictably than volatile agents.
Nitrous oxide suppresses cortical sensory evoked potentials.

questions.expl: SSEPs assess afferent sensory conduction and cortical responses, so neuromuscular blockade does not materially suppress them (unlike motor evoked potentials). Volatiles, nitrous oxide and propofol attenuate SSEP signals dose-dependently.
questions.note: Anki incorrectly mixed SSEPs and MEPs and keyed opioids; this reconstruction uses the physiology of SSEPs.

questions.stem: Suxamethonium may be safely given to patients with

opts.why: GBS denervation creates acetylcholine receptor upregulation and serious potassium release risk.

opts.t: Cerebral palsy without active denervation or muscle degeneration

opts.why: Duchenne dystrophinopathy can cause lethal hyperkalaemic rhabdomyolysis.

opts.t: Major burns several weeks after injury
opts.why: Weeks after major burns, receptor upregulation makes suxamethonium unsafe.

questions.expl: Suxamethonium is generally avoided with dystrophinopathies, denervation after GBS and delayed major-burn physiology because of potentially life-threatening hyperkalaemia. Stable cerebral palsy without active denervation is less clearly associated with this risk.
questions.note: Individual assessment remains necessary; severe immobility and denervation change the safety profile.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man presents to the preadmission clinic two weeks prior to his total knee replacement. His blood results include haemoglobin 100 g/L, ferritin 20 µg/L and normal C-reactive protein. The best course of action is to

opts.t: Proceed without addressing Hb 100 g/L and ferritin 20 microgram/L
opts.why: Ignoring documented iron-deficiency anaemia misses treatable perioperative risk.

opts.t: Give routine blood salvage for the knee replacement instead of investigating
opts.why: Cell salvage cannot replace workup/iron therapy before an elective joint case.

opts.t: Postpone elective surgery to investigate and treat iron-deficiency anaemia

opts.why: Transfusion to 150 g/L is unnecessary and exposes the patient to harm at Hb 100.

questions.expl: Haemoglobin 100 g/L with ferritin 20 microgram/L and normal CRP is clear iron-deficiency anaemia. Elective joint surgery allows investigation of underlying blood loss and iron replacement (oral or IV depending time). Transfusion is not usually required solely for Hb 100.
questions.note: Exact management may differ according to urgency and iron-supplement strategy.

questions.stem: A patient’s glomerular filtration rate is estimated at 35 mL/min/1.73m2. The patient’s chronic kidney disease can be classified as Stage

opts.why: G1 requires eGFR ≥90, not 35.
G5 denotes kidney failure with GFR under 15, not 35.
G2 denotes 60–89, well above this patient's value.

questions.expl: An eGFR of 35 mL/min/1.73m2 lies in the KDIGO G3b band of 30–44. G3a is 45–59, G4 is 15–29 and G5 below 15.

questions.stem: To allow cardiopulmonary bypass in a patient with heparin resistance, fresh frozen plasma may be administered in order to increase the level of

opts.why: Factor VII deficiency is not the mechanism of heparin resistance during CPB.
Factor XI is not heparin's requisite circulating cofactor.
Thrombin is the target neutralised by antithrombin–heparin, not a component to replace.

questions.expl: Unfractionated heparin works through antithrombin. Antithrombin deficiency can cause heparin resistance during cardiopulmonary bypass; antithrombin concentrate or FFP may restore anticoagulant response.

opts.why: A favourable confidence interval to the superior side contradicts inferiority.

Non-inferior but with no evidence of superiority

questions.stem: A patient is undergoing treatment for a malignant hyperthermia crisis. Active cooling should be ceased when the patient’s core temperature has dropped to

opts.why: Cooling to 34°C risks excessive hypothermia in the crisis.

opts.t: When core temperature falls to 38 degrees Celsius

opts.why: 35°C also overshoots the recommended cessation point.
Waiting to 36°C prolongs cooling and can cause avoidable overshoot hypothermia.

questions.expl: During malignant hyperthermia treatment, active cooling is stopped at around 38 degrees to avoid overshoot hypothermia while definitive dantrolene and supportive care continue.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman is to undergo an elective total hip replacement. Her past medical history includes hypertension, stroke, type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic atrial fibrillation and chronic renal impairment with an estimated creatinine clearance of 46 mL/min. Her medications include dabigatran 150 mg bd for stroke prevention. Perioperatively, her dabigatran therapy should

opts.t: Stop only 24 hours before neuraxial anaesthesia
opts.why: 24 hours is insufficient dabigatran clearance in moderate renal dysfunction before neuraxial puncture.

opts.t: Bridge routinely with therapeutic heparin in all AF patients
opts.why: Routine bridging increases bleeding risk and is not recommended for every AF patient.

opts.t: Stop dabigatran about five days before neuraxial anaesthesia with CrCl 46 mL/min
Continue full-dose dabigatran until the day of spinal anaesthesia
opts.why: Continuing dabigatran risks spinal/epidural haematoma during neuraxial blockade.

questions.note: Guidelines have evolved and decisions depend on neuraxial use and thrombotic risk.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with carcinoid syndrome having a resection of a peripheral hepatic metastasis develops a sudden fall in BP from 110/70 mmHg to 85/50 mmHg without significant bleeding. The most appropriate management is

opts.t: Repeated adrenaline boluses as first-line without assessing carcinoid crisis
opts.why: Repeated epinephrine alone without considering carcinoid crisis may worsen mediator-related instability or miss specific treatment.
Reducing tumour stimulation may help but does not replace prompt haemodynamic/octreotide management.

opts.t: No vasoactive treatment despite sustained hypotension
opts.why: Persistent hypotension threatens perfusion and requires active resuscitation.

questions.expl: Sudden hypotension during manipulation of carcinoid metastasis suggests carcinoid crisis; octreotide has historically been the standard initial disease-specific treatment, while haemodynamic support and correction of other causes remain important. Contemporary crisis literature also supports vasopressors when needed.
questions.note: Historical exam strategy; current care uses vasopressors and octreotide according to response.

questions.stem: The nerve(s) that need to be blocked with local anaesthetic to achieve complete anaesthesia for amputation of the fifth toe is/are

opts.why: Lateral femoral cutaneous supplies thigh skin, not toe digital innervation.
Femoral nerve supplies anterior thigh/saphenous medial leg, not the whole fifth toe.
Saphenous alone supplies medial foot, not lateral fifth-toe dorsal and plantar surfaces.

questions.expl: Fifth-toe anaesthesia requires dorsal cutaneous supply from the superficial peroneal nerve and plantar digital supply from the tibial nerve; the other nerves do not collectively cover the little toe.

questions.stem: A man has symptomatic carbon monoxide poisoning. His pulse oximetry (SpO2) and arterial blood gas (PaO2) would be expected to show

opts.t: Reliable low SpO2 on standard two-wavelength oximetry
opts.why: Standard two-wavelength SpO₂ may read falsely normal because COHb resembles oxyHb optically.

opts.t: Falsely normal or high SpO2 with normal PaO2
Low PaO2 necessarily proportional to carboxyhaemoglobin
opts.why: PaO₂ measures dissolved O₂ and can stay normal despite high COHb.

opts.t: Higher-than-normal PaO2 caused by CO binding
opts.why: CO binding to haemoglobin does not cause supranormal dissolved arterial oxygen pressure.

questions.expl: Standard pulse oximeters cannot differentiate oxyhaemoglobin from carboxyhaemoglobin and may appear falsely reassuring, while PaO2 reflects dissolved oxygen tension and can be normal despite severe CO poisoning. Co-oximetry measures COHb.

questions.stem: Venous air embolism during frontal craniotomy is most likely to arise from the

opts.why: MCA is arterial, not the venous source of air entrainment.

opts.t: Superior sagittal sinus or adjacent dural venous sinus

opts.why: Frontal sinus is air-containing but not the large low-pressure vascular source in this scenario.
ICA is a pressurised artery and would bleed rather than entrain atmospheric air under ordinary conditions.

questions.expl: Open non-collapsible dural venous sinuses and bridging veins in the operative field are a recognised source of venous air entry, particularly when the surgical site is elevated above the right atrium.

questions.stem: St. John’s wort (herbal medicine Hypericum perforatum) will reduce the effects of

opts.why: Protamine acts by binding heparin, not CYP metabolism affected by St John's wort.
IV vitamin K is a supplement/reversal of warfarin rather than a CYP-cleared substrate reduced in this way.
Aspirin's irreversible platelet action is not universally abolished by CYP/P-gp induction.

questions.expl: St John's wort induces hepatic CYP enzymes and P-glycoprotein, increasing metabolism of warfarin and reducing its anticoagulant effect. The other therapies are not comparably reduced through this mechanism.
