questions.stem: You are about to anaesthetise a 25-year-old man for an open appendicectomy. He has a history of tricuspid atresia for which he has had a Fontan procedure. An important goal in managing his ventilation under anaesthesia is to ensure

opts.t: Large tidal volumes with high peak pressure
opts.why: High tidal volumes/airway pressure impede passive Fontan pulmonary venous inflow.

opts.t: High ventilation pressures to increase pulmonary blood flow
opts.why: Raising mean intrathoracic pressure reduces venous return and may decrease Fontan flow.

opts.t: High PEEP and long inspiratory time
opts.why: Excess PEEP/long inspiratory time maintains elevated intrathoracic pressure and impairs flow.

opts.t: Short inspiratory time and prolonged expiration with low mean intrathoracic pressure

questions.expl: Fontan circulation depends on passive venous pulmonary blood flow. Limiting mean intrathoracic pressure with low PEEP, short inspiration and adequate expiratory time helps maintain venous return and pulmonary flow.

questions.stem: According to the ‘Fourth Consensus Guidelines for the Management of Postoperative Nausea and Vomiting (PONV)’ published in 2020, multimodal PONV prophylaxis should be implemented in adult patients

opts.t: All adults irrespective of risk and contraindications
opts.why: Guidelines recommend risk-based prophylaxis, not truly every adult irrespective of risks or contraindications.

opts.t: Only patients with a history of severe PONV
opts.why: Waiting for severe previous PONV would withhold prophylaxis from many at-risk patients.

opts.t: Only patients with four or more risk factors
opts.why: A four-risk-factor threshold is too restrictive; one factor now justifies multimodal prophylaxis.

opts.t: Adults with at least one risk factor for PONV

questions.expl: The 2020 Fourth Consensus PONV Guidelines recommend multimodal prophylaxis for adult patients with one or more risk factors. The threshold is deliberately lower than older risk-stratification approaches.

questions.stem: Of the following, the drug that is LEAST likely to provide effective analgesia following paediatric tonsillectomy is

opts.why: Paracetamol is a core recommended tonsillectomy analgesic.
IV dexamethasone reduces postoperative pain and PONV.

opts.t: Clonidine, compared with guideline-supported tonsillectomy analgesics

opts.why: NSAIDs such as ibuprofen provide effective multimodal postoperative analgesia.

questions.expl: The PROSPECT tonsillectomy guideline supports paracetamol, NSAIDs and IV dexamethasone as routine effective perioperative analgesic components. Evidence for clonidine is limited compared with these core interventions.
questions.note: Recalled original distractors included ketamine, which has evidence in children and is not the best exception.

questions.stem: You are anaesthetising a patient for implantation of an automated implantable cardioverter defibrillator. The patient is a 48-year-old with dilated cardiomyopathy and pulmonary hypertension. The preoperative echocardiogram report states that the estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure is 55 mmHg, and that there is mild right ventricular systolic dysfunction. To avoid worsening right ventricular function during induction, it would be best to consider using

opts.t: Carefully titrated dobutamine support when myocardial contractility is inadequate

opts.why: Large dopamine doses may cause tachycardia/arrhythmia and worsen pulmonary vascular loading.

opts.t: Large rapid propofol bolus without vasopressor readiness
opts.why: Rapid propofol can severely depress SVR and cardiac function in unstable cardiomyopathy.
Unopposed high-dose adrenaline risks tachyarrhythmia and increased myocardial oxygen demand.

questions.expl: Dobutamine can enhance RV contractility in pulmonary hypertension, though it may reduce SVR and right-coronary perfusion and must be used cautiously. Vasopressin or noradrenaline are often helpful when systemic pressure is low; no one infusion is universally optimal at induction.
questions.note: The recall deck's dobutamine option is accepted for reconstructed choices; clinical practice also prioritises perfusion pressure and avoidance of raised PVR.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old man complains of left calf pain for two weeks. His pain is worse on walking but not completely relieved by sitting or lying down. On examination, he has mild weakness of left big toe extension. The most likely finding on MRI would be

opts.t: Isolated S1 root compression from a lower disc
opts.why: S1 lesions weaken plantarflexion and affect lateral-foot sensation, not primarily great-toe extension.

opts.t: L4–L5 posterolateral disc herniation affecting the traversing L5 root

opts.why: L3 pathology preferentially weakens knee extension and affects anterior thigh.

opts.t: L5–S1 central disc herniation affecting the traversing S1 root
opts.why: Central L5–S1 disease commonly affects the traversing S1 root, not L5 EHL myotome.

questions.expl: Weakness of great-toe extension localises principally to the L5 myotome. The common disc lesion is L4–L5 impinging the traversing L5 root; a far-lateral L5–S1 lesion could also affect the exiting L5 root.
questions.note: Anki recalled L5/S1, which requires a far-lateral location and was not specified; common posterolateral L4/L5 is anatomically best supported.

questions.stem: A normal sized six-year-old girl has a haemoglobin of 70 g/L following surgery. The volume of packed red blood cells that you would plan to infuse to raise her haemoglobin to 80 g/L is

opts.why: 200 mL would raise Hb far more than 10 g/L in a typical 20-kg child.

opts.t: About 80 mL packed red blood cells

opts.why: 20 mL is only 1 mL/kg and usually produces a smaller Hb increment.
400 mL is excessive for a desired 10-g/L rise and risks volume overload.

questions.expl: For a normal-sized six-year-old (~20 kg), approximately 4 mL/kg of packed red cells raises haemoglobin by about 10 g/L. Hence 20 × 4 = 80 mL. The exact increment depends on product haematocrit and circulating volume.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome is having anaesthesia for a knee arthroscopy. During the procedure he develops the following rhythm. His blood pressure is 100/65 mmHg. The most appropriate treatment is

opts.t: Adenosine for stable regular narrow-complex orthodromic AVRT
IV verapamil for irregular pre-excited AF

A stable regular perfusing rhythm does not require unsynchronised defibrillation without assessment.
Digoxin enhances accessory conduction risk in pre-excited AF and should be avoided.

questions.expl: Regular narrow-complex orthodromic AVRT in a stable WPW patient may be treated with vagal manoeuvres then adenosine. AV-nodal blockers are dangerous in irregular wide-complex pre-excited AF, when procainamide or cardioversion is preferred.

questions.stem: The train-of-four (TOF) ratio above which the majority of anaesthetists will NOT be able to visually detect fade on TOF stimulation is

opts.why: Visual/tactile fade is not reliable up to 0.9; it often becomes undetectable much earlier.
At 0.1 the fade is pronounced and readily visible/tactile.
A TOF ratio above 1 is not required for fade to become visually imperceptible.

questions.expl: Visual or tactile evaluation of TOF fade is very insensitive: many observers cannot perceive fade when the ratio exceeds about 0.4. Quantitative monitoring is required to confirm recovery at least 0.9.

questions.stem: A high mixed venous oxygen saturation (SvO2) is most likely to be associated with

opts.why: Hypovolaemia increases tissue extraction, lowering SvO₂.
Low cardiac output after MI reduces oxygen delivery and usually lowers SvO₂.
Massive PE/shock limits systemic delivery, producing low rather than high mixed venous saturation.

opts.t: High-output sepsis with reduced tissue oxygen extraction

questions.expl: High SvO2 occurs when delivery exceeds extraction, including distributive sepsis with microcirculatory dysfunction and impaired extraction. Low-flow shock states more often increase oxygen extraction and reduce SvO2.

questions.stem: You have anaesthetised a 25-year-old woman for a sleeve gastrectomy. She normally takes the oral contraceptive pill. You used rocuronium and at the end of the case reversed it with 4 mg/kg of sugammadex. Prior to discharge you should advise her to use non-hormonal contraception for the next

opts.t: Seven days of additional non-hormonal contraception

opts.why: One-day backup is too short after sugammadex with hormonal contraception.
Two days is shorter than product advice's seven days.
Twenty-eight days applies to certain other interactions, not standard sugammadex contraception advice.

questions.expl: Sugammadex binds steroidal molecules and may reduce hormonal contraception effectiveness; product information recommends a backup non-hormonal contraceptive method for seven days after administration.

opts.why: AHI below or around one is normal/borderline, not moderate paediatric OSA.
